# Perf: NER token backend batch + throughput

## Goal
Make nym's default NER token-classification backend dramatically faster for the
agent-session scrubbing / datatinder workload (many small chunks in one process).

## Status / Evidence (commit 8d34025)
Root cause found and fixed: decide_one() re-created the Detector (and thus
reloaded the ~138 MB ONNX model) on EVERY chunk, making --jsonl batch mode
pointless (2s per chunk was model load, not inference). Fixed by hoisting
Detector construction to once-per-process (build_decide_detector) and passing
&Detector to decide_one(). Also set with_intra_threads(available_parallelism).

Benchmarks (M2 Ultra, NER-only token backend):
- 60 tiny chunks: ~120s -> 4.1s
- 100 med chunks: ~282s -> 4.4s
- 1000 med chunks: timed out (145 done) -> 25s  (~30-80x)
Correctness intact (multilingual NER + decision output verified); 83 engine tests pass.

## Remaining work (this issue)
1. Batch multiple chunks into one padded [N, seq] forward pass in ner_token.rs
   (new detect_batch), to amortize any remaining per-call ONNX overhead across
   chunks. Cross-platform root fix.
2. Re-benchmark to confirm the batch gain.

## Proof a positive outcome
- cargo test --features decision engine:: all pass.
- time nym decide --jsonl --config <ner.toml> < <1000 chunks> completes and is at
  least ~2x faster than the current path on the same 1000 small chunks.

# Perf: CUDA / TensorRT execution provider for the NER token backend

## Goal
Wire the CUDA (and TensorRT) execution provider into nym's default NER
token-classification backend so NVIDIA boxes (4090, rtx6000) run ONNX NER on the
GPU instead of CPU.

## Background
The default token backend (ner_token.rs) used a bare Session::builder() with no
execution provider. The ner-cuda / ner-tensorrt features only accelerated the
GLiNER path via gline-rs, NOT the default token backend. Add ort/cuda (and
ort/tensorrt) to the ner-cuda / ner-tensorrt features and register the
CUDAExecutionProvider / TensorRtExecutionProvider in the token-backend session
builder under #[cfg(...)], mirroring the CoreML wiring (commit 3adcd87).

## Evidence so far (Apple Silicon, commit 3adcd87)
CoreML EP wired and working, but benchmarked SLOWER than CPU for batch-of-1 on
M2 Ultra (60 tiny chunks 4.5s CPU vs 8.0s CoreML; 1000 med chunks 25s CPU vs
CoreML timed out at 120s). Documented honestly in docs/ner-backends.md. CUDA is
expected to differ (much lower per-call overhead than CoreML) but must be
measured, not assumed.

## Proof a positive outcome
- On a CUDA box (4090 or rtx6000), build with --features ner-cuda and run:
  time nym decide --jsonl --config <ner.toml> < <1000 chunks>
  Must be faster than the CPU-only build on the same box/input, and nvidia-smi
  should show the process using the GPU during the run.

# Perf: CoreML EP for NER token backend (measured slower for batch-of-1)

## Status / Result (commit 3adcd87) - CLOSED with finding
Wired the CoreMLExecutionProvider into the NER token backend (previously
ner-coreml only accelerated GLiNER). Verified working on M2 Ultra, but measured
SLOWER than CPU for the batch-of-1 spans this CLI produces:
- 60 tiny chunks: 4.5s CPU vs 8.0s CoreML (1.8x slower)
- 1000 med chunks: 25s CPU vs CoreML timed out at 120s
Root cause: CoreML per-call overhead (lazy model conversion, ANE dispatch, graph
setup for a single tiny input) exceeds the compute saved.
Kept as opt-in; documented honest caveat in docs/ner-backends.md. The dominant
Apple Silicon win was the model-loaded-once fix + with_intra_threads.

## Recommendation
Keep CPU + with_intra_threads as the Apple Silicon default. CoreML is best
reserved for large-batch / large-input work where the EP fixed cost amortizes.

# Perf: CUDA / TensorRT execution provider for the NER token backend

## Status (commit 736d1f0) - DONE, validated on 4090
Wired CUDAExecutionProvider + TensorRtExecutionProvider into the NER token
backend (ner-cuda/ner-tensorrt features now enable ort/cuda and ort/tensorrt),
mirroring the CoreML wiring.

## Validation (RTX 4090, CUDA 12.8)
Getting the EP to actually engage was non-trivial:
- onnxruntime-gpu 1.30 requires CUDA 13 + cuDNN 9 (not present; box has CUDA 12.8)
  -> EP silently fell back to CPU.
- Pinned onnxruntime-gpu 1.20 + nvidia-cudnn-cu12 + nvidia-cublas-cu12; the EP now
  engages (providers: [CUDAExecutionProvider, CPUExecutionProvider]).
CUDA genuinely accelerates: 5000 medium chunks 56.4s CPU -> 2.7s CUDA (~21x),
output byte-identical to CPU.

## Critical bug found + fixed during validation (sub-batch OOM)
detect_batch padded ALL chunks into one [N, seq] tensor, which OOMs the CUDA
allocator (and can fail large CPU inputs). Added MAX_BATCH_SIZE (128) sub-batching.
This also means an earlier "3s CUDA" was misleading (batched NER was silently
OOM-failing); with the bound CUDA is genuinely ~21x faster (7373 commit's parent
vs 736d1f0).

## TODO (optional follow-ups)
- TensorRT path not benchmarked (needs TensorRT runtime); falls back to CUDA/CPU.
- Document the CUDA result in docs/ner-backends.md (done in commit).

## Proof a positive outcome
- 5000 medium chunks: CPU 56.4s vs CUDA 2.7s (~21x), diff outputs identical.
- 40000 chunks complete without OOM on both CPU and CUDA.
